name: time

attributes.attribute: began at sundown for the Celts
began at the feast of Samhain on November 1
split into summer and winter, each into a beginning and an end

sources: Brunaux, Jean Louis. The Celtic Gauls: Gods, Rites and Sanctuaries. London: Seaby, 1988, 45-48.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Time is not the same for every culture. The Celtic calendar shows what the Celts valued. Each day began at sundown of what we call the previous day. Just as night comes before day, so winter came before spring. The year began with the feast of Samhain held on the first day of November. The year was divided not into four seasons but into two. These were summer and winter. Each of these was split into a beginning and an end. A lunar year counted twelve months of between twenty-nine and thirty days. That gave a year of about three hundred fifty-four days. An extra month was added every two and a half years. This kept the calendar in step with the sun. Some ritual duties were tied to the turning of the seasons and the holy days.

okr.objective: Record the Celtic reckoning of time.
key_results: The Celtic day began at sundown
The year began at Samhain on November 1
The year was split into summer and winter
An extra month was added every two and a half years
